Body mass index in US adults

Dataset 10: NHANES adults (2009-10 and 2011-12 extract)

RSR feasibility analysis

2026-08-03

Introduction

The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) is a continuous cross-sectional survey of the civilian non-institutionalised US population that pairs a household interview with a standardised examination, including measured height and weight. This teaching extract holds 488 adults aged 21 to 80 from the 2009-10 and 2011-12 cycles. Body mass index is the standard population measure of adiposity and the proximal risk factor for type 2 diabetes, hypertension and several cancers, so identifying which social and behavioural characteristics track with it is a standard descriptive epidemiology question.

Aim. Among these US adults, we examined which of age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, income-to-poverty ratio, recreational physical activity, sleep duration, smoking history and self-rated general health are independently associated with BMI, mutually adjusting for the others.

This is a Purpose 3 analysis: several predictors are of interest and the question is which remain associated with the outcome after mutual adjustment.

Methods

Data source. NHANES 2009-10 and 2011-12, a complex multistage probability sample of the US civilian non-institutionalised population. This extract contains 488 adults with 31 variables. Height and weight were measured in the mobile examination centre, not self-reported.

Variables. The outcome is bmi, body mass index in kg/m2, treated as continuous. Predictors are age (years), sex (reference female), race/ethnicity (reference White, the largest group), education (reference College Grad, the largest group), income-to-poverty ratio (household income as a multiple of the federal poverty line), recreational moderate or vigorous physical activity (reference no), usual sleep hours per night, ever having smoked 100 cigarettes (reference no) and self-rated general health collapsed to three levels (reference Excellent/Very good).

Three variables are deliberately excluded. weight_kg and height_cm are excluded because bmi is exactly weight_kg / (height_cm/100)^2 in this file - the largest absolute discrepancy across all rows is 0.05 kg/m2, which is pure rounding - so including any two of the three produces a deterministic relationship and a meaningless model. obese is excluded because it is exactly bmi >= 30 on every row where BMI is observed; regressing BMI on a dichotomised copy of itself is circular.

Statistical analysis. lm(), justified because the outcome is continuous. We fitted a univariable model for each predictor first, then a single multivariable model containing all of them. Predictors were chosen in advance on subject-matter grounds, not by significance. Significance threshold 0.05; estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals. Assumptions were checked with performance::check_model(), and because non-constant variance was flagged we additionally report HC3 heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors. Models are unweighted: the NHANES survey weights, strata and primary sampling units are not carried in this extract, so no result here is a nationally representative estimate. Analysis used R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) with tidyverse, gtsummary and performance.

Missing data. Complete-case analysis: 410 of 488 rows were analysed (78 dropped). The main cost is general_health (48 missing) and poverty_ratio (38 missing). Only 172 of 488 rows are complete on every variable in the file, so listwise deletion is a live threat and the complete-case N is reported for every model.

Median BMI sits in the overweight range with a long right tail reaching beyond 60 kg/m2. The sample is predominantly White and skews toward the more educated categories, with roughly half reporting recreational physical activity and about a third rating their health as no better than Good.

Self-rated health is the strongest crude predictor: compared with participants rating their health Excellent or Very good, those rating it Good average 3.41 kg/m2 (95% CI 2.00 to 4.81) higher BMI (p <0.001) and those rating it Fair or Poor average 4.91 kg/m2 (95% CI 2.91 to 6.91) higher (p <0.001). Recreational physical activity is associated with -2.14 kg/m2 (95% CI -3.48 to -0.80) (p = 0.002) lower BMI, each unit of income-to-poverty ratio with -0.57 kg/m2 (95% CI -0.99 to -0.15) (p = 0.008), and men average -1.43 kg/m2 (95% CI -2.78 to -0.08) (p = 0.038) relative to women. Participants in the “Other” race category average -5.57 kg/m2 (95% CI -9.04 to -2.10) (p = 0.002) lower BMI than White participants. Age, education, sleep hours and smoking show no crude association.

Why adjustment is needed

Income-to-poverty ratio is a clear confounder of the education and race/ethnicity associations: education and income are strongly correlated in this sample, and higher income is associated with lower BMI, so part of any crude education gradient is really an income gradient. Self-rated general health is the other variable that must be handled explicitly - it is associated with income, education and physical activity (people who are poorer, less educated and inactive rate their health worse) and it is strongly associated with BMI, so it will absorb part of every socioeconomic and behavioural coefficient. Note that the causal direction here is ambiguous: high BMI plausibly causes worse self-rated health, in which case adjusting for it is adjusting for a mediator rather than a confounder, and the adjusted activity and income coefficients are correspondingly hard to interpret. Age confounds the sleep and activity associations, since older participants sleep and exercise differently and BMI varies with age. Mutual adjustment lets each coefficient be read as a comparison between participants alike on the other measured characteristics, with the mediation caveat kept in view.

The model explains 14.3% of the variance in BMI (adjusted R-squared 0.108). The gap between R-squared and adjusted R-squared is noticeable because the model spends 16 parameters on 410 observations, many of them on category contrasts that contribute little. Among participants of the same age, sex, race, education, income, activity, sleep and smoking status, rating one’s health as Good rather than Excellent/Very good is associated with 3.12 kg/m2 (95% CI 1.67 to 4.57) higher BMI (p <0.001), and Fair/Poor with 4.73 kg/m2 (95% CI 2.55 to 6.91) higher (p <0.001). Physical activity remains associated with -1.65 kg/m2 (95% CI -3.03 to -0.26) (p = 0.020). Participants in the “Other” race group average -5.65 kg/m2 (95% CI -9.05 to -2.25) (p = 0.001) and Hispanic participants 3.47 kg/m2 (95% CI 0.17 to 6.78) (p = 0.040) relative to White participants. Age, sex, education, income, sleep and smoking are not independently associated. These are associations among the participants observed, not effects of intervening.

Two predictors move meaningfully toward the null and lose significance. Sex falls from -1.43 kg/m2 (95% CI -2.78 to -0.08) crude to -0.41 kg/m2 (95% CI -1.74 to 0.92) adjusted, and income-to-poverty ratio from -0.57 kg/m2 (95% CI -0.99 to -0.15) to -0.30 kg/m2 (95% CI -0.77 to 0.18) - in both cases the crude estimate was carrying self-rated health and education, which are correlated with both. Physical activity attenuates but survives, from -2.14 kg/m2 (95% CI -3.48 to -0.80) to -1.65 kg/m2 (95% CI -3.03 to -0.26), so part but not all of the crude activity difference was socioeconomic and health-status confounding. By contrast, the two general- health contrasts barely move at all (Good: 3.41 kg/m2 (95% CI 2.00 to 4.81) to 3.12 kg/m2 (95% CI 1.67 to 4.57); Fair/Poor: 4.91 kg/m2 (95% CI 2.91 to 6.91) to 4.73 kg/m2 (95% CI 2.55 to 6.91)), and race “Other” is essentially unchanged (-5.57 kg/m2 (95% CI -9.04 to -2.10) to -5.65 kg/m2 (95% CI -9.05 to -2.25)) - these are not explained by the other measured characteristics. One estimate crosses into significance: Hispanic ethnicity goes from 3.68 kg/m2 (95% CI 0.31 to 7.05) (p = 0.032) to 3.47 kg/m2 (95% CI 0.17 to 6.78) (p = 0.040), which with n = 17 Hispanic participants is a fragile finding rather than a discovery.

The diagnostics are the weakest part of this analysis. The posterior-predictive check shows the model cannot reproduce the long right tail of the BMI distribution: observed BMI is strongly right-skewed and the fitted normal predictive distribution is symmetric. The residual-versus-fitted panel fans out markedly, and check_heteroscedasticity() confirms non-constant error variance (p < 0.001). The normal-QQ panel shows a pronounced heavy right tail, and check_normality() also rejects. Collinearity is the highest of any model in this dataset but still acceptable: the largest VIF is 2.09 for education, followed by 1.76 for race/ethnicity and 1.40 for income-to-poverty ratio. The first two are four-degree-of-freedom terms, and the correlation between education and income is the substantive reason for the inflation; nothing here approaches the conventional VIF threshold of 5. A small number of very obese participants sit near the Cook’s distance contours but none dominates the fit.

Because variance is non-constant, Table 3 reports HC3 robust standard errors. The HC3 SE for the Fair/Poor health contrast is 1.309 against an OLS SE of 1.109, i.e. wider, which is the expected direction when the worse-health group also has more variable BMI. The substantive conclusions do not change: the general-health contrasts, race “Other” and physical activity keep their significance status under robust inference. A log or square-root transformation of BMI would address both the skew and much of the heteroscedasticity, at the cost of interpreting coefficients on a multiplicative scale.

Discussion

In this NHANES extract, worse self-rated general health is the characteristic most strongly and independently associated with higher BMI - roughly 3.1 kg/m2 for Good and 4.7 kg/m2 for Fair/Poor relative to Excellent/Very good - followed by lower BMI among the physically active. The crude sex and income differences are fully explained by the other measured characteristics. Practically, self-rated health is a single question that identifies a group averaging several BMI units higher, which is useful for targeting, but the association is very likely bidirectional and should not be read as health perception causing weight.

Limitations. The models are unweighted, and the NHANES sampling weights, strata and PSUs are not in this extract, so the sample must not be described as nationally representative. The design is cross-sectional, so temporality is unknown; in particular, adjusting for self-rated general health is probably adjusting for a consequence of high BMI, which biases the remaining coefficients in an unpredictable direction - this is over-adjustment, not confounder control. Physical activity is a crude yes/no self-report with no intensity or duration, and reverse causation is likely (high BMI reduces exercise). Diet, which is the dominant determinant of BMI, is not measured at all. Complete-case analysis dropped 78 of 488 rows (16%). Residual variance is non-constant and residuals are strongly non-normal; HC3 SEs address inference but not the model’s inability to predict the obese tail. Hispanic (n = 17) and Other (n = 16) groups are small, so those contrasts are unstable. All estimates are associations, not causal effects.

Future work. Refit on log(BMI) with the NHANES survey design and dietary recall variables from the full public files, and drop self-rated health from the adjustment set to avoid conditioning on a mediator.

Feasibility notes

NOT part of a student report.

  • Usable but not the strongest choice. The signal is real but almost entirely carried by general_health, which is arguably a consequence of BMI rather than a cause. A student who does not spot the mediation issue will write a confidently wrong discussion.
  • Trap: obese must never be a predictor here. obese is exactly bmi >= 30 on all 485 rows where BMI is observed (the 3 apparent exceptions are rows where BMI itself is missing, so obese is missing too). Including it yields an R-squared near 0.6 that means nothing.
  • Trap: weight_kg and height_cm must be excluded. bmi is exactly weight_kg/(height_cm/100)^2 (max discrepancy 0.05 kg/m2). Any two of the three in one model is a deterministic relationship.
  • Failed diagnostics. Heteroscedasticity p < 0.001 and non-normality p < 0.001, both driven by the long right tail of BMI. HC3 fixes inference; it does not fix the fit. This is a good teaching case for transformation, but a student who reports untransformed BMI with a straight face has an assumption violation on the record.
  • Low explained variance (R-squared 0.143, adjusted 0.108). The 16 parameters buy very little; the adjusted-versus-raw gap is worth pointing out.
  • Complete-case N 410 of 488 (16% lost), driven by general_health (10% missing) and poverty_ratio (8% missing).
  • Small race cells. Hispanic 17, Other 16 in the analytic sample; the Hispanic coefficient flips into significance on adjustment and should not be trusted.
  • Unweighted survey analysis. Must be stated in Methods and Limitations.
  • No separation (linear model). Highest collinearity of the four linear models (max VIF 2.09, education; race 1.76; poverty_ratio 1.40) but well short of a threshold that would require action.
